name: Otis W. Smith
bio: Dr. Otis W. Smith was the only Negro physician in Ft. Valley, Georgia. After a crossed telephone line led to an exchange of angry words with a white woman in 1958, he was sentenced to eight months on a work gang and fined $500 — the sentence suspended only on condition that he write the woman a letter begging forgiveness and leave town. The case became a national emblem of Jim-Crow justice.
charges: 'Using abusive language' — a crossed telephone-line argument with a white woman
convicted: Sentenced to eight months on a work gang and $500 fine; suspended on condition he apologize and leave town
sentence: 8 months on a work gang and $500 fine (suspended on humiliating conditions)

name: Clennon King
bio: Clennon King was a Black college professor who in June 1958 tried to register for graduate study at the all-white University of Mississippi. State authorities seized him and committed him to the state mental hospital at Whitfield for a psychiatric examination — on the theory that any Negro who tried to integrate Ole Miss must be insane. He was held about twelve days before being released.
charges: Committed to a state mental hospital after attempting to register at the University of Mississippi
sentence: Held about 12 days in the state mental hospital at Whitfield

name: Hanover Thompson
bio: James Hanover Thompson was a nine-year-old boy at the center of the 'Kissing Case' in Monroe, North Carolina. In October 1958, after a white girl kissed him on the cheek during a children's game, he and seven-year-old David 'Fuzzy' Simpson were arrested, held days without counsel, tried for 'attempted rape,' and committed to a reform school on indeterminate sentences. International protest — and a defense led by Robert F. Williams and the NAACP — won their release in early 1959.
charges: 'Attempted rape' / assault on females (a white girl kissed him during a game)
convicted: Held in jail without counsel, then committed to the Morrison Training School
sentence: Indeterminate juvenile sentence to reform school; released in early 1959 after worldwide protest

name: David Simpson
bio: David 'Fuzzy' Simpson was a seven-year-old boy arrested with nine-year-old Hanover Thompson in the 1958 'Kissing Case' in Monroe, North Carolina, after a white girl kissed Thompson during a game. Charged with 'attempted rape,' the two children were jailed and committed to the Morrison Training School for an indeterminate term. A worldwide outcry and the NAACP's Robert F. Williams secured their release in early 1959.
charges: 'Attempted rape' / assault on females (tied to the children's kissing game)
convicted: Jailed without counsel, then committed to the Morrison Training School
sentence: Indeterminate juvenile sentence to reform school; released in early 1959

name: Fred Shuttlesworth
affiliation: Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights
bio: The Rev. Fred L. Shuttlesworth was president of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and a founder of the SCLC. After thirteen of his followers were jailed on Oct. 20, 1958 for sitting in the front seats of Birmingham buses to defy a new segregation ordinance, he was charged with fostering a conspiracy, convicted on four misdemeanor counts, fined $100 and sentenced to 90 days.
charges: Conspiracy / inciting — the Birmingham bus-desegregation protest

name: J. S. Phifer
affiliation: Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights
bio: The Rev. J. S. Phifer was an associate of Fred Shuttlesworth in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, tried with him in 1958 over the Birmingham bus-desegregation protest in which thirteen riders were jailed for refusing to move from the front seats. Phifer was fined $100 and given a 60-day sentence.
charges: Bus-segregation ordinance / conspiracy — the Birmingham bus protest

name: Edward T. Graham
bio: The Rev. Edward T. Graham was a Miami minister and NAACP leader, one of four witnesses cited for contempt by the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee — the segregationist 'Johns Committee' — when he refused to answer its questions in a 1958 probe aimed at crippling the NAACP amid the school-integration fight.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee
convicted: Cited for refusing to answer the committee
sentence: Cited for contempt; resisted the anti-NAACP probe

name: G. E. Graves
bio: G. E. Graves Jr. was an NAACP attorney in Miami, cited for contempt by the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee (the 'Johns Committee') when he refused to answer its questions during the 1958 hearings that sought to expose and dismantle the NAACP in the wake of school desegregation.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee
convicted: Cited for refusing to answer the committee

name: Bertha Teplow
bio: Mrs. Bertha Teplow was one of the first witnesses cited for contempt by the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee (the 'Johns Committee') on the opening day of its 1958 Miami hearings, after she refused to answer questions in the segregationist body's probe into the NAACP and alleged subversion in the integration movement.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee
convicted: Cited for refusing to answer the committee

name: Anna Rosenblatt
bio: Anna Rosenblatt was cited for contempt with Bertha Teplow on the first day of the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee's 1958 Miami hearings, for refusing to answer the segregationist 'Johns Committee' as it probed the NAACP and alleged Communist influence in the school-integration struggle.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee
convicted: Cited for refusing to answer the committee

name: W. C. Patton
bio: W. C. Patton was an official of the Alabama State Coordinating Association for Registration and Voting. In 1958 Alabama Attorney General John Patterson sought to brand him and William P. Mitchell as covert agents of the banned NAACP and brought an additional contempt case against them in the state courts — part of Alabama's drive to suppress Black voter-registration work.
charges: State contempt proceedings — alleged to be a covert agent of the banned NAACP
sentence: Prosecuted in Alabama's campaign against the NAACP and Black voter registration

name: William P. Mitchell
bio: William P. Mitchell was an official of the Alabama State Coordinating Association for Registration and Voting, named with W. C. Patton in a 1958 Alabama contempt case after the state attorney general accused them of secretly serving the banned NAACP. The prosecution was part of Alabama's effort to choke off Black voter-registration organizing.
charges: State contempt proceedings — alleged to be a covert agent of the banned NAACP
sentence: Prosecuted in Alabama's campaign against the NAACP and Black voter registration
